name: Semax

track.title: Lab & animal
track.line: Rat and mouse studies, mostly in Russia

track.title: Pilot in people
track.line: Small Russian studies, nasal drops only

track.title: Phase I

track.title: FDA approval

what.text: Semax is a chain of seven amino acids: Met-Glu-His-Phe-Pro-Gly-Pro. Its molecular weight is about 814 daltons. It is sold as a free base or an acetate salt. It is a common name, not an official drug name.

It is a synthetic analog of a fragment of the hormone ACTH (ACTH 4-10), without ACTH’s hormone effects. Its Pro-Gly-Pro end is thought to slow its breakdown. It was made at the Institute of Molecular Genetics of the Russian Academy of Sciences.
In Russia it is a registered medicine, sold as 0.1% and 1% nasal drops, according to FDA’s 2026 review of Russia’s state drug register.
How it acts, according to animal studies:

items.text: In rats with induced strokes, it reduced brain damage; in one study the damaged area was about 20% smaller.
In rats, it raised nerve growth factors (BDNF and NGF) in the brain within an hour.
In rats, it made blood clot less (anticoagulant and antithrombotic effects).
In rodents, it raised pain thresholds when injected, but not when given in the nose, in one study.
In mice, it boosted the dopamine release caused by amphetamine. FDA flags this as a possible abuse concern.

what.text: FDA describes its mechanisms as poorly understood. Animal effects have not been confirmed in people.
Adonis does not carry Semax today.

research.text: Human evidence: small studies, almost all from Russia and many published only in Russian, all with nasal drops. For the uses it reviewed, FDA found two usable references, both small and uncontrolled. FDA found no study of Semax given by injection.

Across eight references, FDA counted Semax use in about 33 to 47 healthy adults, 69 adults with medical conditions and 451 children with depression or tics. Three were meeting abstracts, and most did not discuss side effects.

research.title: Migraine and facial nerve pain, 1996

facts.v: Koroleva et al. 1996, as summarized by FDA
no blinding, no control group
12 adults with migraine, 16 with trigeminal neuralgia and 9 with dental plexalgia
one dose of Semax in the nose
an undescribed pain rating scale, and nerve and blood-flow recordings up to 30 minutes after

research.found: Migraine: 4 of 12 said the headache stopped 90 to 120 minutes later. Typical trigeminal neuralgia: no change. The authors concluded that Semax "does not exhibit analgesic activity by itself." They reported no side effects.

research.title: Acute ischemic stroke, 1997 (Russia)

facts.v: Gusev EI, et al. Zh Nevrol Psikhiatr Im S S Korsakova 1997;97(6):26-34 (in Russian)
Semax added to standard care, compared with patients on standard care alone. The abstract does not describe randomization or blinding.
30 patients on Semax; 80 controls with similar strokes
5- or 10-day courses
clinical rating scales, EEG and evoked potentials

research.found: The authors report "some influence" on the speed of recovery of neurological function, especially movement.

src.label: Gusev et al., Zh Nevrol Psikhiatr, 1997

research.title: Stroke rehabilitation, 2018 (Russia)

facts.v: Gusev EI, et al. Zh Nevrol Psikhiatr Im S S Korsakova 2018;118(3):61-68 (in Russian)
early and late rehabilitation groups, each split into Semax and no-Semax subgroups. The abstract does not describe randomization or blinding.
110 adults after ischemic stroke (43 men, 67 women, mean age 58)
two 10-day courses, followed for about 5 months
BDNF in blood, muscle strength, Barthel daily-living score

research.found: The authors report higher BDNF levels and better Barthel scores with Semax, with less effect on weakness.

src.label: Gusev et al., Zh Nevrol Psikhiatr, 2018

research.title: Brain scans in healthy volunteers, 2018

facts.v: Lebedeva IS, et al. Bull Exp Biol Med 2018;165(5):653-656
Semax or placebo, compared between two groups
24 healthy volunteers (11 men, 13 women, mean age 44): 14 on Semax, 10 on placebo
one dose of 1% Semax nasal drops, or placebo
scans before and 5 and 20 minutes after
resting-state functional MRI of the default mode network

research.found: One part of the network, in the medial frontal cortex, was larger in the Semax group. No clinical outcome was measured.

src.label: Lebedeva et al., Bull Exp Biol Med, 2018

research.text: FDA did not consider Russian-only stroke papers, because full English versions were not available. The one stroke reference it reviewed was a meeting abstract that gave no patient count and no clinical outcomes.
No Semax trial was found on ClinicalTrials.gov.

Rat and mouse studies, mostly from Russian groups, report less brain damage after induced stroke, more nerve growth factors, less blood clotting, pain relief when injected, and antidepressant- and anxiety-reducing effects. FDA notes they mostly used one fixed dose and did not measure how much reached the blood. No published toxicity studies were found.

items.text: FDA’s scientists, in a memo dated May 11, 2026 for the July meeting, recommended against adding Semax (free base or acetate) to the compounding list. They found insufficient evidence of effectiveness for cerebral ischemia, migraine or trigeminal neuralgia, and raised safety and quality concerns for injected and nasal-spray forms.
Semax was also nominated for ADHD and as a "nootropic". FDA did not evaluate ADHD because no supporting literature was found.

FDA’s advisory committee voted on Semax on July 24, 2026: 8 in favor of adding it to the compounding list, 5 against and 1 abstaining, in both forms, as reported by Healio from the July 23–24, 2026 meeting. FDA has not posted the official vote record.

src.label: Healio, "FDA committee recommends looser restrictions for several peptides"

us.text: Not FDA-approved for any use. Since October 30, 2026, HHS has said it will not take enforcement action against licensed pharmacies and physicians that compound Semax free base for use in the nose (intranasal), under set conditions. That is enforcement discretion, not approval. As of October 31, 2026.

items.text: none. Semax has no USP or National Formulary monograph.
FDA lists "Semax (heptapeptide)" among substances previously in Category 2 whose nominations were withdrawn. FDA wrote that it has no or limited safety information for the proposed routes.
Wells Pharmacy Network and LDT Health Solutions nominated it for nasal spray or injection; both withdrew. FDA reviewed it on its own initiative.

HHS announced an enforcement discretion policy on October 28, 2026, published in the Federal Register on October 30, 2026 (Docket HHS-OASH-2026-0496). It names Semax free base, for use in the nose (intranasal). HHS says it does not intend to take enforcement action against state-licensed pharmacies, federal facilities or licensed physicians that compound it when every condition is met. As of October 31, 2026.

items.text: a licensed pharmacist or physician compounds it; the bulk substance matches the listed peptide and route; it comes from an FDA-registered maker that follows good manufacturing practice, with a valid certificate of analysis; there is a valid patient-specific prescription; the product contains only one active ingredient from the list; serious adverse events and quality problems are reported to FDA's MedWatch and state authorities; the label says "This is a compounded drug product. Not for resale."; oral forms have documented adequate bioavailability; the only device packaged with it is an FDA-cleared syringe; and all other section 503A requirements are met.

src.label: BakerHostetler summary of the HHS policy (a law firm's summary, used because HHS's own policy appendix could not be opened)

items.text: The policy does not make it FDA approved. It does not cover blends with other active ingredients, other routes or forms, outsourcing facilities (section 503B), or products sold as research chemicals or dietary supplements. It is interim and not binding: HHS may revise or withdraw it, in whole or in part, if safety signals or product-quality problems appear.

items.text: no outsourcing facility has reported compounding Semax since 2019. FDA found clinics and online sellers marketing injections and nasal sprays, some labelled "for research purposes only". FDA also cites a federal press release about a Kentucky pharmacy that compounded and distributed Semax products from October 2018 to April 2020.
no. It is not on the DEA’s controlled substances list dated October 21, 2026.

us.text: Compounded drugs are not FDA-approved. FDA does not review their safety, effectiveness or quality before they are sold.

world.lead: Russia is the one country where Semax is a registered medicine, as nasal drops, according to FDA’s review of the Russian register. No approval was found elsewhere, and EMA lists no Semax medicine. WADA does not name it.

countries.status: Not approved. Compounding under HHS enforcement discretion since Oct 30, 2026, for Semax free base by use in the nose (intranasal) only.

after.title: Sport
after.text: Semax is not named on the WADA Prohibited List for 2026 or 2027. WADA’s class S0 bans at all times any pharmacological substance with no current approval by any government health regulator for human use. For 2027, WADA warned that peptides not named on the List may still fall under S0 or other classes. The lists do not say whether Semax is covered.
Australia: Semax is not named in the Poisons Standard (June 2026). The TGA’s product register was not checked.

side.text: Side-effect data are sparse. Most Semax studies did not report on side effects, and there are no human pharmacokinetic data. FDA flagged a possible bleeding risk, a possible abuse concern from animal work, and one serious consumer report.

items.text: one small study reported no side effects; the others did not discuss them. No safety data exist for injection.

one report through December 3, 2025. A consumer had eye pain and burning after using Semax 0.1% nasal drops bought online in May 2024, was hospitalized, and still had eye pain a year later. A report like this does not show that Semax caused it.
Semax reduced blood clotting in rats. FDA says this raises concern about bleeding, especially with other drugs that raise bleeding risk.
in mice it boosted amphetamine-triggered dopamine release, a response typical of drugs of abuse. No studies have assessed abuse potential.
FDA is concerned about immune reactions to injected or sprayed Semax from clumping and peptide impurities.

unconfirmed: Russia’s state drug register (grls.rosminzdrav.ru) loaded but asks for a picture code before showing results, so Semax’s register entry could not be opened; its Russian status comes from FDA’s briefing, which cites that register (accessed by FDA Dec 4, 2025).
Koroleva et al. 1996 and the Russian-language stroke papers were not opened in full; the 1996 study is reported as FDA summarized it.
Canada (the Drug Product Database connection failed), UK (MHRA) and Australia’s TGA register were not checked.
Vote counts come from Healio's report of the July 23–24, 2026 meeting; FDA has not posted the official vote record.
surprises: Semax is marketed in the US as injections and nasal sprays, but its Russian registration is for nasal drops, and FDA found no study of injected Semax.
A 2022 Russian review says Semax does not cause drug dependence; FDA notes that in mice it boosted amphetamine-triggered dopamine release and that no study has assessed its abuse potential.
Semax is sold online for pain, but in the only pain study FDA found, the authors concluded it "does not exhibit analgesic activity by itself."
Semax is marketed for ADHD, anxiety, depression, Parkinson’s and Alzheimer’s disease; FDA found no literature supporting ADHD and did not evaluate the others.
